Figure 2. Dependence of $\Sigma_{tot}(\tau)=\sigma(\tau)/\sigma_{0}$ on $\tau$ for Q=1 (solid curve), Q=2 (dashed curve) and Q=3 (dotted curve).

The total cross section increases with $Q$ and is well approximated at $Q \gg 1$ by the formula

$$
\sigma (\tau) \approx \pi \sigma_ {0} \ln (1 + 2 Q | \cos \tau |).
$$

The total cross section averaged over time may also be of interest,

$$
\overline {{\sigma}} (Q) = \int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi} \sigma (\tau) \frac {d \tau}{2 \pi} = \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {1} [ 1 - J _ {0} (Q y) ] \frac {d y}{y}. \tag {21}
$$

\sigma_{a}(\vartheta,\tau)/d\vartheta$ on $\vartheta$ for several values of f.

It follows from the asymptotics obtained that for alternating current the total scattering cross section $\sigma(\tau)$ is finite, in contrast to the case of direct current. The main contribution to $\sigma(\tau)$ is given by the region of scattering angles $\theta \sim \theta_{0} (\vartheta \sim 1)$ . We have from (12) for $v/c \ll 1$ ,

$$
\sigma (\tau) = \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {+ \infty} d y [ 1 - \cos \Xi_ {1} (y, \tau) ]
$$

$$
= \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {Q | \cos \tau |} (1 - \cos y) \frac {d y}{y}. \tag {20}
$$

Naturally, there is no asymmetry in $\sigma(\tau)$ . The dependence of $\Sigma_{tot}(\tau)=\sigma(\tau)/\sigma_{0}$ on $\tau$ is shown in Fig.2 for several values of Q.

, while $G_{2}(\vartheta, \tau)$ does not change sign. For convenience, in Eq. (16) we have passed from the angle $\theta$ to $\vartheta$ .

If $\vartheta \gg 1$ ( $1 \gg \theta \gg \theta_0$ ), then

$$
d \sigma (\vartheta , \tau) = \sigma_ {0} \sin^ {2} (Q \cos \tau) \frac {d \vartheta}{\vartheta^ {2}}. \tag {17}
$$

For $\vartheta \ll 1$ ( $\theta \ll \theta_0$ ), we have

$$
d \sigma (\vartheta , \tau) = \sigma_ {0} \left| \int_ {0} ^ {Q | \cos \tau |} (1 - \cos y) \frac {d y}{y} \right| ^ {2} d \vartheta .

Figure 2. Dependence of $\Sigma_{tot}(\tau)=\sigma(\tau)/\sigma_{0}$ on $\tau$ for Q=1 (solid curve), Q=2 (dashed curve) and Q=3 (dotted curve).

The total cross section increases with $Q$ and is well approximated at $Q \gg 1$ by the formula

$$
\sigma (\tau) \approx \pi \sigma_ {0} \ln (1 + 2 Q | \cos \tau |).
$$

The total cross section averaged over time may also be of interest,

$$
\overline {{\sigma}} (Q) = \int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi} \sigma (\tau) \frac {d \tau}{2 \pi} = \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {1} [ 1 - J _ {0} (Q y) ] \frac {d y}{y}. \tag {21}
$$

The dependence of $\overline{\Sigma}_{tot}(Q) = \overline{\sigma}(Q) / \sigma_0$ on $Q$ is shown in

\sigma_{a}(\vartheta,\tau)/d\vartheta$ on $\vartheta$ for several values of f.

It follows from the asymptotics obtained that for alternating current the total scattering cross section $\sigma(\tau)$ is finite, in contrast to the case of direct current. The main contribution to $\sigma(\tau)$ is given by the region of scattering angles $\theta \sim \theta_{0} (\vartheta \sim 1)$ . We have from (12) for $v/c \ll 1$ ,

$$
\sigma (\tau) = \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {+ \infty} d y [ 1 - \cos \Xi_ {1} (y, \tau) ]
$$

$$
= \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {Q | \cos \tau |} (1 - \cos y) \frac {d y}{y}. \tag {20}
$$

Naturally, there is no asymmetry in $\sigma(\tau)$ . The dependence of $\Sigma_{tot}(\tau)=\sigma(\tau)/\sigma_{0}$ on $\tau$ is shown in Fig.2 for several values of Q.

, while $G_{2}(\vartheta, \tau)$ does not change sign. For convenience, in Eq. (16) we have passed from the angle $\theta$ to $\vartheta$ .

If $\vartheta \gg 1$ ( $1 \gg \theta \gg \theta_0$ ), then

$$
d \sigma (\vartheta , \tau) = \sigma_ {0} \sin^ {2} (Q \cos \tau) \frac {d \vartheta}{\vartheta^ {2}}. \tag {17}
$$

For $\vartheta \ll 1$ ( $\theta \ll \theta_0$ ), we have

$$
d \sigma (\vartheta , \tau) = \sigma_ {0} \left| \int_ {0} ^ {Q | \cos \tau |} (1 - \cos y) \frac {d y}{y} \right| ^ {2} d \vartheta .

stage=initial_expandedrank=9query_text=At τ≈3, order Σ_tot(τ) by Q from highest to lowest.node_id=bad4486a9b70f8e94b4a5b409d3ffdb4:text:11:part:0point_id=57af5b85-82fc-51ec-963d-bf959542ea2ddoc_id=bad4486a9b70f8e94b4a5b409d3ffdb4source=data\demo_docs\2412.16030_Non-stationary_Aharonov-Bohm_effect.pdftitle=2412.16030_Non-stationary_Aharonov-Bohm_effectpage=3chunk_index=11modality=textchannel=textvector_name=nullparser_name=minerusource_parser=mineruscore=0.1211score_vector=0.0000score_bm25=nullscore_rrf=nullrerank_score=nullscore_composite=0.1211score_policy=inherited_relationship_v1threshold_passed=nullexpanded_from=bad4486a9b70f8e94b4a5b409d3ffdb4:text:12expansion_relation=prev_idcandidate_pool=contextexpansion_mode=routedexpansion_allowed_by=context_text_thresholdseed_rank=1seed_threshold=0.5relation_priority=60replaced_relation=nullagent_relevance_score=nullagent_relevance_label=nullagent_relevance_keep=nullagent_relevance_drop=nullagent_label_score_delta=nullagent_related_modality_delta=nullagent_related_context_text_delta=nullagent_related_context_node_id=nullagent_related_context_present=nullagent_related_context_added=nullagent_related_context_fixed_score=nullagent_relevance_reasoning=null
rerank_score=null
\tag {17}
$$

For $\vartheta \ll 1$ ( $\theta \ll \theta_0$ ), we have

$$
d \sigma (\vartheta , \tau) = \sigma_ {0} \left| \int_ {0} ^ {Q | \cos \tau |} (1 - \cos y) \frac {d y}{y} \right| ^ {2} d \vartheta . \tag {18}
$$

The asymptotics (17) and (18) for the cross sections are independent of $s = \operatorname{sgn}(q)$ , since either the function $G_{1}(\vartheta, \tau)$ contributes to the cross section for $\vartheta \gg 1$ , or $G_{2}(\vartheta, \tau)$ for $\vartheta \ll 1$ . However, for $\vartheta \sim 1$ an asymmetry arises due to the interference of the functions $G_{1}(\vartheta, \tau)$ and $G_{2}(\vartheta, \tau)$ . This asymmetry will be an alternating function of $\tau$ and can be observed by measuring the non-stationary Hall effect (oscillating voltage in the transverse direction).

Let us represent the cross section $d\sigma(\vartheta, \tau)$ in (16) in the form

$$
d \sigma (\vartheta , \tau) = d \sigma_ {s} (\vartheta , \tau) + s d \sigma_ {a} (\vartheta , \tau),
$$

$$
d \sigma_ {s} (\theta , \tau) = \sigma_ {0} \left[ G _ {1} ^ {2} (\vartheta , \tau) + \frac {1}{\vartheta^ {2}} G _ {2} ^ {2} (\vartheta , \tau) \right] d \vartheta ,
$$

$$
d \sigma_ {a} (\theta , \tau) = 2 \sigma_ {0} G _ {1} (\vartheta , \tau) G _ {2} (\vartheta , \tau) \frac {d \vartheta}{\vartheta}. \tag {19}
$$

The functions $G_{1}(\vartheta,\tau)$ and $G_{2}(\vartheta,\tau)$ depend on the parameter Q and variable $\tau$ only through the combination $f = Q\cos\tau$ . Fig. 1 shows the dependence of $\Sigma_{s}(\vartheta,\tau) = \sigma_{0}^{-1}d\sigma_{s}(\vartheta,\tau)/d\vartheta$ and $\Sigma_{a}(\vartheta,\tau) = \sigma_{0}^{-1}d\sigma_{a}(\vartheta,\tau)/d\vartheta$ on $\vartheta$ for several values of f.

Figure 3. Dependence of $\overline{\Sigma}_{tot} = \overline{\sigma}(Q) / \sigma_0$ on $Q$ .

mically with increasing $Q$ for large $Q$ .

# III. CONCLUSION

The non-stationary Aharonov-Bohm effect is investigated in the non-relativistic approximation. Using the eikonal approach, the differential and total scattering cross sections are found. In contrast to the stationary Aharonov-Bohm effect, the total cross section in the non-stationary case is finite. The main contribution to the scattering cross section comes from the angles $\theta \sim \theta_{0} = \hbar\omega/E \ll 1$ . The differential scattering cross section contains an asymmetry with respect to the replacement $q \rightarrow -q$ . This asymmetry has a maximum at $\theta \sim \theta_{0}$ and decreases rapidly at $\theta \gg \theta_{0}$ and $\theta \ll \theta_{0}$ . The asymmetry in the cross section can be observed as the non-stationary Hall effect, and the total scattering cross section manifests itself in oscillations of the total electron flux.

# ACKNOWLEDGEMENT

The work of Ivan Terekhov was financially supported by the ITMO Fellowship Program.

[2] M. Peshkin and A. Tonomura, The Aharonov-Bohm Effect, Lecture Notes in Physics 340 (Springer-Verlag, Berlin, 1989).   
[3] B. Lee, E. Yin, T. K. Gustafson, R. Chiao, Analysis of Aharonov-Bohm effect due to time-dependent vector potentials, Phys. Rev. A 45, 4319 (1992).   
[4] A. N. Ageev, S. Yu. Davydov, and A. G. Chirkov, Magnetic Aharonov-Bohm effect under time-dependent vector potential, Pis'ma v Zhurnal Tekhnicheskoi Fiziki, 9, 70 (2000) [Technical Physics Letters 26, 392 (2000)].   
[5] B. Gaveau, A. M. Nounou, L. S.

Naturally, there is no asymmetry in $\sigma(\tau)$ . The dependence of $\Sigma_{tot}(\tau)=\sigma(\tau)/\sigma_{0}$ on $\tau$ is shown in Fig.2 for several values of Q.

![](images/1b7ffdcf3a86d09e9a2953e40a0196a8b8d4ea16c8d7eab29b8b93214871675a.jpg)

Figure 1. Dependence of $\Sigma_{s}(\vartheta,\tau)=\sigma_{0}^{-1}d\sigma_{s}(\vartheta,\tau)/d\vartheta$ (top plot) and $\Sigma_{a}(\vartheta,\tau)=\sigma_{0}^{-1}d\sigma_{a}(\vartheta,\tau)/d\vartheta$ (bottom plot) on $\vartheta$ for f=2 (solid curve), f=3 (dashed curve) and f=4 (dotted curve), $f=Q\cos\tau$ .   
![](images/11b6cb6bb6e89aace75756a2cc1fe8d9b6b31902b1ce08266c810ecedfead7f2.jpg)

<details>
<summary>line</summary>


</details>

Figure 2. Dependence of $\Sigma_{tot}(\tau)=\sigma(\tau)/\sigma_{0}$ on $\tau$ for Q=1 (solid curve), Q=2 (dashed curve) and Q=3 (dotted curve).

The total cross section increases with $Q$ and is well approximated at $Q \gg 1$ by the formula

$$
\sigma (\tau) \approx \pi \sigma_ {0} \ln (1 + 2 Q | \cos \tau |).
$$

The total cross section averaged over time may also be of interest,

$$
\overline {{\sigma}} (Q) = \int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi} \sigma (\tau) \frac {d \tau}{2 \pi} = \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {1} [ 1 - J _ {0} (Q y) ] \frac {d y}{y}. \tag {21}
$$

The dependence of $\overline{\Sigma}_{tot}(Q) = \overline{\sigma}(Q) / \sigma_0$ on $Q$ is shown in

Fig. 3. The time-averaged cross section grows logarith-

\sigma_{a}(\vartheta,\tau)/d\vartheta$ on $\vartheta$ for several values of f.

It follows from the asymptotics obtained that for alternating current the total scattering cross section $\sigma(\tau)$ is finite, in contrast to the case of direct current. The main contribution to $\sigma(\tau)$ is given by the region of scattering angles $\theta \sim \theta_{0} (\vartheta \sim 1)$ . We have from (12) for $v/c \ll 1$ ,

$$
\sigma (\tau) = \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {+ \infty} d y [ 1 - \cos \Xi_ {1} (y, \tau) ]
$$

$$
= \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {Q | \cos \tau |} (1 - \cos y) \frac {d y}{y}. \tag {20}
$$

Naturally, there is no asymmetry in $\sigma(\tau)$ . The dependence of $\Sigma_{tot}(\tau)=\sigma(\tau)/\sigma_{0}$ on $\tau$ is shown in Fig.2 for several values of Q.

!

, while $G_{2}(\vartheta, \tau)$ does not change sign. For convenience, in Eq. (16) we have passed from the angle $\theta$ to $\vartheta$ .

If $\vartheta \gg 1$ ( $1 \gg \theta \gg \theta_0$ ), then

$$
d \sigma (\vartheta , \tau) = \sigma_ {0} \sin^ {2} (Q \cos \tau) \frac {d \vartheta}{\vartheta^ {2}}. \tag {17}
$$

For $\vartheta \ll 1$ ( $\theta \ll \theta_0$ ), we have

$$
d \sigma (\vartheta , \tau) = \sigma_ {0} \left| \int_ {0} ^ {Q | \cos \tau |} (1 - \cos y) \frac {d y}{y} \right| ^ {2} d \vartheta .

Formula (display): d \sigma (\theta , \tau) = \frac {\hbar}{2 \pi P} \left| \int_ {- \infty} ^ {+ \infty} d y e ^ {- i s y} \left[ 1 - e ^ {- i \Xi (y, \tau)} \right] \right| ^ {2} \frac {d \theta}{\theta^ {2}},

\Xi (y, \tau) = \frac {\zeta y Q}{2} \int_ {- \infty} ^ {\infty} \frac {d z}{r} \left[ J _ {1} (\zeta r) \sin (\phi) - N _ {1} (\zeta r) \cos (\phi) \right],

\zeta = \frac {k}{| q |} = \frac {\hbar k}{P \theta}, Q = \frac {e \Phi_ {0}}{2 c \hbar}, \phi = \tau + \frac {c}{v} \zeta z,

r = \sqrt {y ^ {2} + z ^ {2}}, \quad s = \operatorname{sgn} q. \tag {13}

Figure 2. Dependence of $\Sigma_{tot}(\tau)=\sigma(\tau)/\sigma_{0}$ on $\tau$ for Q=1 (solid curve), Q=2 (dashed curve) and Q=3 (dotted curve).

The total cross section increases with $Q$ and is well approximated at $Q \gg 1$ by the formula

$$
\sigma (\tau) \approx \pi \sigma_ {0} \ln (1 + 2 Q | \cos \tau |).
$$

The total cross section averaged over time may also be of interest,

$$
\overline {{\sigma}} (Q) = \int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi} \sigma (\tau) \frac {d \tau}{2 \pi} = \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {1} [ 1 - J _ {0} (Q y) ] \frac {d y}{y}. \tag {21}
$$

The dependence of $\overline{\Sigma}_{tot}(Q) = \overline{\sigma}(Q) / \sigma_0$ on $Q$ is shown in

\sigma_{a}(\vartheta,\tau)/d\vartheta$ on $\vartheta$ for several values of f.

It follows from the asymptotics obtained that for alternating current the total scattering cross section $\sigma(\tau)$ is finite, in contrast to the case of direct current. The main contribution to $\sigma(\tau)$ is given by the region of scattering angles $\theta \sim \theta_{0} (\vartheta \sim 1)$ . We have from (12) for $v/c \ll 1$ ,

$$
\sigma (\tau) = \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {+ \infty} d y [ 1 - \cos \Xi_ {1} (y, \tau) ]
$$

$$
= \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {Q | \cos \tau |} (1 - \cos y) \frac {d y}{y}. \tag {20}
$$

Naturally, there is no asymmetry in $\sigma(\tau)$ . The dependence of $\Sigma_{tot}(\tau)=\sigma(\tau)/\sigma_{0}$ on $\tau$ is shown in Fig.2 for several values of Q.

# 文章：什么时候该用 $< \mathrm{a}>$ ？

当你的意图是“导航到某个资源”时，用链接很合适；如果是触发动作（比如打开弹窗），通常更该用<button>。

小提示：你也可以用链接跳到页面内的某个位置，比如跳到联系信息。

Naturally, there is no asymmetry in $\sigma(\tau)$ . The dependence of $\Sigma_{tot}(\tau)=\sigma(\tau)/\sigma_{0}$ on $\tau$ is shown in Fig.2 for several values of Q.

![](images/1b7ffdcf3a86d09e9a2953e40a0196a8b8d4ea16c8d7eab29b8b93214871675a.jpg)

Figure 1. Dependence of $\Sigma_{s}(\vartheta,\tau)=\sigma_{0}^{-1}d\sigma_{s}(\vartheta,\tau)/d\vartheta$ (top plot) and $\Sigma_{a}(\vartheta,\tau)=\sigma_{0}^{-1}d\sigma_{a}(\vartheta,\tau)/d\vartheta$ (bottom plot) on $\vartheta$ for f=2 (solid curve), f=3 (dashed curve) and f=4 (dotted curve), $f=Q\cos\tau$ .   
![](images/11b6cb6bb6e89aace75756a2cc1fe8d9b6b31902b1ce08266c810ecedfead7f2.jpg)

<details>
<summary>line</summary>


</details>

Figure 2. Dependence of $\Sigma_{tot}(\tau)=\sigma(\tau)/\sigma_{0}$ on $\tau$ for Q=1 (solid curve), Q=2 (dashed curve) and Q=3 (dotted curve).

The total cross section increases with $Q$ and is well approximated at $Q \gg 1$ by the formula

$$
\sigma (\tau) \approx \pi \sigma_ {0} \ln (1 + 2 Q | \cos \tau |).
$$

The total cross section averaged over time may also be of interest,

$$
\overline {{\sigma}} (Q) = \int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi} \sigma (\tau) \frac {d \tau}{2 \pi} = \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {1} [ 1 - J _ {0} (Q y) ] \frac {d y}{y}. \tag {21}
$$

The dependence of $\overline{\Sigma}_{tot}(Q) = \overline{\sigma}(Q) / \sigma_0$ on $Q$ is shown in

\sigma_{a}(\vartheta,\tau)/d\vartheta$ on $\vartheta$ for several values of f.

It follows from the asymptotics obtained that for alternating current the total scattering cross section $\sigma(\tau)$ is finite, in contrast to the case of direct current. The main contribution to $\sigma(\tau)$ is given by the region of scattering angles $\theta \sim \theta_{0} (\vartheta \sim 1)$ . We have from (12) for $v/c \ll 1$ ,

$$
\sigma (\tau) = \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {+ \infty} d y [ 1 - \cos \Xi_ {1} (y, \tau) ]
$$

$$
= \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {Q | \cos \tau |} (1 - \cos y) \frac {d y}{y}. \tag {20}
$$

Naturally, there is no asymmetry in $\sigma(\tau)$ . The dependence of $\Sigma_{tot}(\tau)=\sigma(\tau)/\sigma_{0}$ on $\tau$ is shown in Fig.2 for several values of Q.

# 文章：什么时候该用 $< \mathrm{a}>$ ？

当你的意图是“导航到某个资源”时，用链接很合适；如果是触发动作（比如打开弹窗），通常更该用<button>。

小提示：你也可以用链接跳到页面内的某个位置，比如跳到联系信息。

\tag {17}
$$

For $\vartheta \ll 1$ ( $\theta \ll \theta_0$ ), we have

$$
d \sigma (\vartheta , \tau) = \sigma_ {0} \left| \int_ {0} ^ {Q | \cos \tau |} (1 - \cos y) \frac {d y}{y} \right| ^ {2} d \vartheta . \tag {18}
$$

The asymptotics (17) and (18) for the cross sections are independent of $s = \operatorname{sgn}(q)$ , since either the function $G_{1}(\vartheta, \tau)$ contributes to the cross section for $\vartheta \gg 1$ , or $G_{2}(\vartheta, \tau)$ for $\vartheta \ll 1$ . However, for $\vartheta \sim 1$ an asymmetry arises due to the interference of the functions $G_{1}(\vartheta, \tau)$ and $G_{2}(\vartheta, \tau)$ . This asymmetry will be an alternating function of $\tau$ and can be observed by measuring the non-stationary Hall effect (oscillating voltage in the transverse direction).

Let us represent the cross section $d\sigma(\vartheta, \tau)$ in (16) in the form

$$
d \sigma (\vartheta , \tau) = d \sigma_ {s} (\vartheta , \tau) + s d \sigma_ {a} (\vartheta , \tau),
$$

$$
d \sigma_ {s} (\theta , \tau) = \sigma_ {0} \left[ G _ {1} ^ {2} (\vartheta , \tau) + \frac {1}{\vartheta^ {2}} G _ {2} ^ {2} (\vartheta , \tau) \right] d \vartheta ,
$$

$$
d \sigma_ {a} (\theta , \tau) = 2 \sigma_ {0} G _ {1} (\vartheta , \tau) G _ {2} (\vartheta , \tau) \frac {d \vartheta}{\vartheta}. \tag {19}
$$

The functions $G_{1}(\vartheta,\tau)$ and $G_{2}(\vartheta,\tau)$ depend on the parameter Q and variable $\tau$ only through the combination $f = Q\cos\tau$ . Fig. 1 shows the dependence of $\Sigma_{s}(\vartheta,\tau) = \sigma_{0}^{-1}d\sigma_{s}(\vartheta,\tau)/d\vartheta$ and $\Sigma_{a}(\vartheta,\tau) = \sigma_{0}^{-1}d\sigma_{a}(\vartheta,\tau)/d\vartheta$ on $\vartheta$ for several values of f.

  "text": "\\tag {17}\n$$\n\nFor $\\vartheta \\ll 1$ ( $\\theta \\ll \\theta_0$ ), we have\n\n$$\nd \\sigma (\\vartheta , \\tau) = \\sigma_ {0} \\left| \\int_ {0} ^ {Q | \\cos \\tau |} (1 - \\cos y) \\frac {d y}{y} \\right| ^ {2} d \\vartheta . \\tag {18}\n$$\n\nThe asymptotics (17) and (18) for the cross sections are independent of $s = \\operatorname{sgn}(q)$ , since either the function $G_{1}(\\vartheta, \\tau)$ contributes to the cross section for $\\vartheta \\gg 1$ , or $G_{2}(\\vartheta, \\tau)$ for $\\vartheta \\ll 1$ . However, for $\\vartheta \\sim 1$ an asymmetry arises due to the interference of the functions $G_{1}(\\vartheta, \\tau)$ and $G_{2}(\\vartheta, \\tau)$ . This asymmetry will be an alternating function of $\\tau$ and can be observed by measuring the non-stationary Hall effect (oscillating voltage in the transverse direction).\n\nLet us represent the cross section $d\\sigma(\\vartheta, \\tau)$ in (16) in the form\n\n$$\nd \\sigma (\\vartheta , \\tau) = d \\sigma_ {s} (\\vartheta , \\tau) + s d \\sigma_ {a} (\\vartheta , \\tau),\n$$\n\n$$\nd \\sigma_ {s} (\\theta , \\tau) = \\sigma_ {0} \\left[ G _ {1} ^ {2} (\\vartheta , \\tau) + \\frac {1}{\\vartheta^ {2}} G _ {2} ^ {2} (\\vartheta , \\tau) \\right] d \\vartheta ,\n$$\n\n$$\nd \\sigma_ {a} (\\theta , \\tau) = 2 \\sigma_ {0} G _ {1} (\\vartheta , \\tau) G _ {2} (\\vartheta , \\tau) \\frac {d \\vartheta}{\\vartheta}. \\tag {19}\n$$\n\nThe functions $G_{1}(\\vartheta,\\tau)$ and $G_{2}(\\vartheta,\\tau)$ depend on the parameter Q and variable $\\tau$ only through the combination $f = Q\\cos\\tau$ . Fig. 1 shows the dependence of $\\Sigma_{s}(\\vartheta,\\tau) = \\sigma_{0}^{-1}d\\sigma_{s}(\\vartheta,\\tau)/d\\vartheta$ and $\\Sigma_{a}(\\vartheta,\\tau) = \\sigma_{0}^{-1}d\\sigma_{a}(\\vartheta,\\tau)/d\\vartheta$ on $\\vartheta$ for several values of f.",

# III. CONCLUSION

The non-stationary Aharonov-Bohm effect is investigated in the non-relativistic approximation. Using the eikonal approach, the differential and total scattering cross sections are found. In contrast to the stationary Aharonov-Bohm effect, the total cross section in the non-stationary case is finite. The main contribution to the scattering cross section comes from the angles $\theta \sim \theta_{0} = \hbar\omega/E \ll 1$ . The differential scattering cross section contains an asymmetry with respect to the replacement $q \rightarrow -q$ . This asymmetry has a maximum at $\theta \sim \theta_{0}$ and decreases rapidly at $\theta \gg \theta_{0}$ and $\theta \ll \theta_{0}$ . The asymmetry in the cross section can be observed as the non-stationary Hall effect, and the total scattering cross section manifests itself in oscillations of the total electron flux.

# ACKNOWLEDGEMENT

The work of Ivan Terekhov was financially supported by the ITMO Fellowship Program.

[1] Y. Aharonov and D. Bohm, Significance of electromagnetic potentials in the Quantum theory, Phys. Rev. 115, 485 (1959).   
[2] M. Peshkin and A. Tonomura, The Aharonov-Bohm Effect, Lecture Notes in Physics 340 (Springer-Verlag, Berlin, 1989).   
[3] B. Lee, E. Yin, T. K. Gustafson, R. Chiao, Analysis of Aharonov-Bohm effect due to time-dependent vector potentials, Phys. Rev. A 45, 4319 (1992).   
[4] A. N. Ageev, S. Yu. Davydov, and A. G. Chirkov, Magnetic Aharonov-Bohm effect under time-dependent vector potential, Pis'ma v Zhurnal Tekhnicheskoi Fiziki, 9, 70 (2000) [Technical Physics Letters 26, 392 (2000)].   
[5] B. Gaveau, A. M. Nounou, L. S.

, the electric and magnetic fields outside the solenoid will be equal to zero.

However, if the current in the solenoid is alternating, the electromagnetic fields will be non-zero in the accessible to the electron motion region. In this case, the topology of the space accessible to the electron motion is the same as that in the stationary case, so that the influence of alternating magnetic field flux inside the solenoid on the electron motion outside the solenoid (the non-stationary Aharonov-Bohm effect) will be somewhat similar to the stationary effect, but will also have some differences. The non-stationary Aharonov-Bohm effect has been discussed in many papers with contradictory results (see, for example, $[3–8]$ ). However, none of these papers calculated such experimentally important quantities as the differential and total scattering cross sections. Our work is devoted to the study of these quantities.

# II. EIKONAL APPROXIMATION AND THE CROSS SECTION OF NON-STATIONARY AHARONOV-BOHM EFFECT

Let us consider an infinitely long solenoid with radius $a$ and the number $n$ of turns per unit length, through which a current $I(t) = I_0 \cos(\omega t)$ is passed. We denote

$$
\Phi_ {0} = \frac {4 \pi^ {2} a ^ {2}}{c} n I _ {0}, \tag {1}
$$

where c is the speed of light. At $\omega = 0$ this quantity coincides with the magnetic field flux through the solenoid. We are interested in the limit $a \rightarrow 0$ at a fixed value of $\Phi_{0}$ .

Figure 2. Dependence of $\Sigma_{tot}(\tau)=\sigma(\tau)/\sigma_{0}$ on $\tau$ for Q=1 (solid curve), Q=2 (dashed curve) and Q=3 (dotted curve).

The total cross section increases with $Q$ and is well approximated at $Q \gg 1$ by the formula

$$
\sigma (\tau) \approx \pi \sigma_ {0} \ln (1 + 2 Q | \cos \tau |).
$$

The total cross section averaged over time may also be of interest,

$$
\overline {{\sigma}} (Q) = \int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi} \sigma (\tau) \frac {d \tau}{2 \pi} = \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {1} [ 1 - J _ {0} (Q y) ] \frac {d y}{y}. \tag {21}
$$

\sigma_{a}(\vartheta,\tau)/d\vartheta$ on $\vartheta$ for several values of f.

It follows from the asymptotics obtained that for alternating current the total scattering cross section $\sigma(\tau)$ is finite, in contrast to the case of direct current. The main contribution to $\sigma(\tau)$ is given by the region of scattering angles $\theta \sim \theta_{0} (\vartheta \sim 1)$ . We have from (12) for $v/c \ll 1$ ,

$$
\sigma (\tau) = \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {+ \infty} d y [ 1 - \cos \Xi_ {1} (y, \tau) ]
$$

$$
= \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {Q | \cos \tau |} (1 - \cos y) \frac {d y}{y}. \tag {20}
$$

Naturally, there is no asymmetry in $\sigma(\tau)$ . The dependence of $\Sigma_{tot}(\tau)=\sigma(\tau)/\sigma_{0}$ on $\tau$ is shown in Fig.2 for several values of Q.

(16) we have passed from the angle $\\theta$ to $\\vartheta$ .\n\nIf $\\vartheta \\gg 1$ ( $1 \\gg \\theta \\gg \\theta_0$ ), then\n\n$$\nd \\sigma (\\vartheta , \\tau) = \\sigma_ {0} \\sin^ {2} (Q \\cos \\tau) \\frac {d \\vartheta}{\\vartheta^ {2}}. \\tag {17}\n$$\n\nFor $\\vartheta \\ll 1$ ( $\\theta \\ll \\theta_0$ ), we have\n\n$$\nd \\sigma (\\vartheta , \\tau) = \\sigma_ {0} \\left| \\int_ {0} ^ {Q | \\cos \\tau |} (1 - \\cos y) \\frac {d y}{y} \\right| ^ {2} d \\vartheta .",

Figure 2. Dependence of $\Sigma_{tot}(\tau)=\sigma(\tau)/\sigma_{0}$ on $\tau$ for Q=1 (solid curve), Q=2 (dashed curve) and Q=3 (dotted curve).

The total cross section increases with $Q$ and is well approximated at $Q \gg 1$ by the formula

$$
\sigma (\tau) \approx \pi \sigma_ {0} \ln (1 + 2 Q | \cos \tau |).
$$

The total cross section averaged over time may also be of interest,

$$
\overline {{\sigma}} (Q) = \int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi} \sigma (\tau) \frac {d \tau}{2 \pi} = \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {1} [ 1 - J _ {0} (Q y) ] \frac {d y}{y}. \tag {21}
$$

\sigma_{a}(\vartheta,\tau)/d\vartheta$ on $\vartheta$ for several values of f.

It follows from the asymptotics obtained that for alternating current the total scattering cross section $\sigma(\tau)$ is finite, in contrast to the case of direct current. The main contribution to $\sigma(\tau)$ is given by the region of scattering angles $\theta \sim \theta_{0} (\vartheta \sim 1)$ . We have from (12) for $v/c \ll 1$ ,

$$
\sigma (\tau) = \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {+ \infty} d y [ 1 - \cos \Xi_ {1} (y, \tau) ]
$$

$$
= \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {Q | \cos \tau |} (1 - \cos y) \frac {d y}{y}. \tag {20}
$$

Naturally, there is no asymmetry in $\sigma(\tau)$ . The dependence of $\Sigma_{tot}(\tau)=\sigma(\tau)/\sigma_{0}$ on $\tau$ is shown in Fig.2 for several values of Q.

, while $G_{2}(\vartheta, \tau)$ does not change sign. For convenience, in Eq. (16) we have passed from the angle $\theta$ to $\vartheta$ .

If $\vartheta \gg 1$ ( $1 \gg \theta \gg \theta_0$ ), then

$$
d \sigma (\vartheta , \tau) = \sigma_ {0} \sin^ {2} (Q \cos \tau) \frac {d \vartheta}{\vartheta^ {2}}. \tag {17}
$$

For $\vartheta \ll 1$ ( $\theta \ll \theta_0$ ), we have

$$
d \sigma (\vartheta , \tau) = \sigma_ {0} \left| \int_ {0} ^ {Q | \cos \tau |} (1 - \cos y) \frac {d y}{y} \right| ^ {2} d \vartheta .

Figure 2. Dependence of $\Sigma_{tot}(\tau)=\sigma(\tau)/\sigma_{0}$ on $\tau$ for Q=1 (solid curve), Q=2 (dashed curve) and Q=3 (dotted curve).

The total cross section increases with $Q$ and is well approximated at $Q \gg 1$ by the formula

$$
\sigma (\tau) \approx \pi \sigma_ {0} \ln (1 + 2 Q | \cos \tau |).
$$

The total cross section averaged over time may also be of interest,

$$
\overline {{\sigma}} (Q) = \int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi} \sigma (\tau) \frac {d \tau}{2 \pi} = \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {1} [ 1 - J _ {0} (Q y) ] \frac {d y}{y}. \tag {21}
$$

It follows from the asymptotics obtained that for alternating current the total scattering cross section $\sigma(\tau)$ is finite, in contrast to the case of direct current. The main contribution to $\sigma(\tau)$ is given by the region of scattering angles $\theta \sim \theta_{0} (\vartheta \sim 1)$ . We have from (12) for $v/c \ll 1$ ,

$$
\sigma (\tau) = \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {+ \infty} d y [ 1 - \cos \Xi_ {1} (y, \tau) ]
$$

$$
= \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {Q | \cos \tau |} (1 - \cos y) \frac {d y}{y}. \tag {20}
$$

Naturally, there is no asymmetry in $\sigma(\tau)$ . The dependence of $\Sigma_{tot}(\tau)=\sigma(\tau)/\sigma_{0}$ on $\tau$ is shown in Fig.2 for several values of Q.

$$

For $\vartheta \ll 1$ ( $\theta \ll \theta_0$ ), we have

$$
d \sigma (\vartheta , \tau) = \sigma_ {0} \left| \int_ {0} ^ {Q | \cos \tau |} (1 - \cos y) \frac {d y}{y} \right| ^ {2} d \vartheta . \tag {18}
$$

The asymptotics (17) and (18) for the cross sections are independent of $s = \operatorname{sgn}(q)$ , since either the function $G_{1}(\vartheta, \tau)$ contributes to the cross section for $\vartheta \gg 1$ , or $G_{2}(\vartheta, \tau)$ for $\vartheta \ll 1$ . However, for $\vartheta \sim 1$ an asymmetry arises due to the interference of the functions $G_{1}(\vartheta, \tau)$ and $G_{2}(\vartheta, \tau)$ . This asymmetry will be an alternating function of $\tau$ and can be observed by measuring the non-stationary Hall effect (oscillating voltage in the transverse direction).

Let us represent the cross section $d\sigma(\vartheta, \tau)$ in (16) in the form

$$
d \sigma (\vartheta , \tau) = d \sigma_ {s} (\vartheta , \tau) + s d \sigma_ {a} (\vartheta , \tau),
$$

$$
d \sigma_ {s} (\theta , \tau) = \sigma_ {0} \left[ G _ {1} ^ {2} (\vartheta , \tau) + \frac {1}{\vartheta^ {2}} G _ {2} ^ {2} (\vartheta , \tau) \right] d \vartheta ,
$$

$$
d \sigma_ {a} (\theta , \tau) = 2 \sigma_ {0} G _ {1} (\vartheta , \tau) G _ {2} (\vartheta , \tau) \frac {d \vartheta}{\vartheta}. \tag {19}
$$

The functions $G_{1}(\vartheta,\tau)$ and $G_{2}(\vartheta,\tau)$ depend on the parameter Q and variable $\tau$ only through the combination $f = Q\cos\tau$ . Fig. 1 shows the dependence of $\Sigma_{s}(\vartheta,\tau) = \sigma_{0}^{-1}d\sigma_{s}(\vartheta,\tau)/d\vartheta$ and $\Sigma_{a}(\vartheta,\tau) = \sigma_{0}^{-1}d\sigma_{a}(\vartheta,\tau)/d\vartheta$ on $\vartheta$ for several values of f.

# III. CONCLUSION

The non-stationary Aharonov-Bohm effect is investigated in the non-relativistic approximation. Using the eikonal approach, the differential and total scattering cross sections are found. In contrast to the stationary Aharonov-Bohm effect, the total cross section in the non-stationary case is finite. The main contribution to the scattering cross section comes from the angles $\theta \sim \theta_{0} = \hbar\omega/E \ll 1$ . The differential scattering cross section contains an asymmetry with respect to the replacement $q \rightarrow -q$ . This asymmetry has a maximum at $\theta \sim \theta_{0}$ and decreases rapidly at $\theta \gg \theta_{0}$ and $\theta \ll \theta_{0}$ . The asymmetry in the cross section can be observed as the non-stationary Hall effect, and the total scattering cross section manifests itself in oscillations of the total electron flux.

[3] B. Lee, E. Yin, T. K. Gustafson, R. Chiao, Analysis of Aharonov-Bohm effect due to time-dependent vector potentials, Phys. Rev. A 45, 4319 (1992).   
[4] A. N. Ageev, S. Yu. Davydov, and A. G. Chirkov, Magnetic Aharonov-Bohm effect under time-dependent vector potential, Pis'ma v Zhurnal Tekhnicheskoi Fiziki, 9, 70 (2000) [Technical Physics Letters 26, 392 (2000)].   
[5] B. Gaveau, A. M. Nounou, L. S.

stage=retry_2_expandedrank=22query_text=At τ≈3, order Σ_tot(τ) by Q from highest to lowest. 图片 图像 图中 image figurenode_id=bad4486a9b70f8e94b4a5b409d3ffdb4:text:6:part:1point_id=2d561057-0c8d-592c-b79d-d33987fc6dbbdoc_id=bad4486a9b70f8e94b4a5b409d3ffdb4source=data\demo_docs\2412.16030_Non-stationary_Aharonov-Bohm_effect.pdftitle=2412.16030_Non-stationary_Aharonov-Bohm_effectpage=1chunk_index=6modality=textchannel=textvector_name=nullparser_name=minerusource_parser=mineruscore=0.0880score_vector=0.0000score_bm25=nullscore_rrf=nullrerank_score=nullscore_composite=0.0880score_policy=inherited_relationship_v1threshold_passed=nullexpanded_from=bad4486a9b70f8e94b4a5b409d3ffdb4:text:11:part:1expansion_relation=page_windowcandidate_pool=routedexpansion_mode=routedexpansion_allowed_by=routed_relationship_thresholdseed_rank=2seed_threshold=0.55relation_priority=20replaced_relation=nullagent_relevance_score=nullagent_relevance_label=nullagent_relevance_keep=nullagent_relevance_drop=nullagent_label_score_delta=nullagent_related_modality_delta=nullagent_related_context_text_delta=nullagent_related_context_node_id=nullagent_related_context_present=nullagent_related_context_added=nullagent_related_context_fixed_score=nullagent_relevance_reasoning=null

, the electric and magnetic fields outside the solenoid will be equal to zero.

However, if the current in the solenoid is alternating, the electromagnetic fields will be non-zero in the accessible to the electron motion region. In this case, the topology of the space accessible to the electron motion is the same as that in the stationary case, so that the influence of alternating magnetic field flux inside the solenoid on the electron motion outside the solenoid (the non-stationary Aharonov-Bohm effect) will be somewhat similar to the stationary effect, but will also have some differences. The non-stationary Aharonov-Bohm effect has been discussed in many papers with contradictory results (see, for example, $[3–8]$ ). However, none of these papers calculated such experimentally important quantities as the differential and total scattering cross sections. Our work is devoted to the study of these quantities.

# II. EIKONAL APPROXIMATION AND THE CROSS SECTION OF NON-STATIONARY AHARONOV-BOHM EFFECT

Let us consider an infinitely long solenoid with radius $a$ and the number $n$ of turns per unit length, through which a current $I(t) = I_0 \cos(\omega t)$ is passed. We denote

$$
\Phi_ {0} = \frac {4 \pi^ {2} a ^ {2}}{c} n I _ {0}, \tag {1}
$$

where c is the speed of light. At $\omega = 0$ this quantity coincides with the magnetic field flux through the solenoid. We are interested in the limit $a \rightarrow 0$ at a fixed value of $\Phi_{0}$ .

Naturally, there is no asymmetry in $\sigma(\tau)$ . The dependence of $\Sigma_{tot}(\tau)=\sigma(\tau)/\sigma_{0}$ on $\tau$ is shown in Fig.2 for several values of Q.

![](images/1b7ffdcf3a86d09e9a2953e40a0196a8b8d4ea16c8d7eab29b8b93214871675a.jpg)

Figure 1. Dependence of $\Sigma_{s}(\vartheta,\tau)=\sigma_{0}^{-1}d\sigma_{s}(\vartheta,\tau)/d\vartheta$ (top plot) and $\Sigma_{a}(\vartheta,\tau)=\sigma_{0}^{-1}d\sigma_{a}(\vartheta,\tau)/d\vartheta$ (bottom plot) on $\vartheta$ for f=2 (solid curve), f=3 (dashed curve) and f=4 (dotted curve), $f=Q\cos\tau$ .   
![](images/11b6cb6bb6e89aace75756a2cc1fe8d9b6b31902b1ce08266c810ecedfead7f2.jpg)

<details>
<summary>line</summary>


</details>

Figure 2. Dependence of $\Sigma_{tot}(\tau)=\sigma(\tau)/\sigma_{0}$ on $\tau$ for Q=1 (solid curve), Q=2 (dashed curve) and Q=3 (dotted curve).

The total cross section increases with $Q$ and is well approximated at $Q \gg 1$ by the formula

$$
\sigma (\tau) \approx \pi \sigma_ {0} \ln (1 + 2 Q | \cos \tau |).
$$

The total cross section averaged over time may also be of interest,

$$
\overline {{\sigma}} (Q) = \int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi} \sigma (\tau) \frac {d \tau}{2 \pi} = \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {1} [ 1 - J _ {0} (Q y) ] \frac {d y}{y}. \tag {21}
$$

The dependence of $\overline{\Sigma}_{tot}(Q) = \overline{\sigma}(Q) / \sigma_0$ on $Q$ is shown in

\sigma_{a}(\vartheta,\tau)/d\vartheta$ on $\vartheta$ for several values of f.

It follows from the asymptotics obtained that for alternating current the total scattering cross section $\sigma(\tau)$ is finite, in contrast to the case of direct current. The main contribution to $\sigma(\tau)$ is given by the region of scattering angles $\theta \sim \theta_{0} (\vartheta \sim 1)$ . We have from (12) for $v/c \ll 1$ ,

$$
\sigma (\tau) = \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {+ \infty} d y [ 1 - \cos \Xi_ {1} (y, \tau) ]
$$

$$
= \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {Q | \cos \tau |} (1 - \cos y) \frac {d y}{y}. \tag {20}
$$

Naturally, there is no asymmetry in $\sigma(\tau)$ . The dependence of $\Sigma_{tot}(\tau)=\sigma(\tau)/\sigma_{0}$ on $\tau$ is shown in Fig.2 for several values of Q.

!

, while $G_{2}(\vartheta, \tau)$ does not change sign. For convenience, in Eq. (16) we have passed from the angle $\theta$ to $\vartheta$ .

If $\vartheta \gg 1$ ( $1 \gg \theta \gg \theta_0$ ), then

$$
d \sigma (\vartheta , \tau) = \sigma_ {0} \sin^ {2} (Q \cos \tau) \frac {d \vartheta}{\vartheta^ {2}}. \tag {17}
$$

For $\vartheta \ll 1$ ( $\theta \ll \theta_0$ ), we have

$$
d \sigma (\vartheta , \tau) = \sigma_ {0} \left| \int_ {0} ^ {Q | \cos \tau |} (1 - \cos y) \frac {d y}{y} \right| ^ {2} d \vartheta .

Naturally, there is no asymmetry in $\sigma(\tau)$ . The dependence of $\Sigma_{tot}(\tau)=\sigma(\tau)/\sigma_{0}$ on $\tau$ is shown in Fig.2 for several values of Q.

![](images/1b7ffdcf3a86d09e9a2953e40a0196a8b8d4ea16c8d7eab29b8b93214871675a.jpg)

Figure 1. Dependence of $\Sigma_{s}(\vartheta,\tau)=\sigma_{0}^{-1}d\sigma_{s}(\vartheta,\tau)/d\vartheta$ (top plot) and $\Sigma_{a}(\vartheta,\tau)=\sigma_{0}^{-1}d\sigma_{a}(\vartheta,\tau)/d\vartheta$ (bottom plot) on $\vartheta$ for f=2 (solid curve), f=3 (dashed curve) and f=4 (dotted curve), $f=Q\cos\tau$ .   
![](images/11b6cb6bb6e89aace75756a2cc1fe8d9b6b31902b1ce08266c810ecedfead7f2.jpg)

<details>
<summary>line</summary>


</details>

Figure 2. Dependence of $\Sigma_{tot}(\tau)=\sigma(\tau)/\sigma_{0}$ on $\tau$ for Q=1 (solid curve), Q=2 (dashed curve) and Q=3 (dotted curve).

The total cross section increases with $Q$ and is well approximated at $Q \gg 1$ by the formula

$$
\sigma (\tau) \approx \pi \sigma_ {0} \ln (1 + 2 Q | \cos \tau |).
$$

The total cross section averaged over time may also be of interest,

$$
\overline {{\sigma}} (Q) = \int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi} \sigma (\tau) \frac {d \tau}{2 \pi} = \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {1} [ 1 - J _ {0} (Q y) ] \frac {d y}{y}. \tag {21}
$$

The dependence of $\overline{\Sigma}_{tot}(Q) = \overline{\sigma}(Q) / \sigma_0$ on $Q$ is shown in

The dependence of $\\Sigma_{tot}(\\tau)=\\sigma(\\tau)/\\sigma_{0}$ on $\\tau$ is shown in Fig.2 for several values of Q.\n\n![](images/1b7ffdcf3a86d09e9a2953e40a0196a8b8d4ea16c8d7eab29b8b93214871675a.jpg)\n\n<details>\n<summary>line</summary>\n\n\n</details>\n\n![](images/6702d0432117e9c2c1065da445998cb9174570bd2d519804540866ab6cf10e5a.jpg)\n\n<details>\n<summary>line</summary>\n\n\n</details>\n\nFigure 1. Dependence of $\\Sigma_{s}(\\vartheta,\\tau)=\\sigma_{0}^{-1}d\\sigma_{s}(\\vartheta,\\tau)/d\\vartheta$ (top plot) and $\\Sigma_{a}(\\vartheta,\\tau)=\\sigma_{0}^{-1}d\\sigma_{a}(\\vartheta,\\tau)/d\\vartheta$ (bottom plot) on $\\vartheta$ for f=2 (solid curve), f=3 (dashed curve) and f=4 (dotted curve), $f=Q\\cos\\tau$ .   \n![](images/11b6cb6bb6e89aace75756a2cc1fe8d9b6b31902b1ce08266c810ecedfead7f2.jpg)\n\n<details>\n<summary>line</summary>\n\n\n</details>\n\nFigure 2. Dependence of $\\Sigma_{tot}(\\tau)=\\sigma(\\tau)/\\sigma_{0}$ on $\\tau$ for Q=1 (solid curve), Q=2 (dashed curve) and Q=3 (dotted curve).\n\nThe total cross section increases with $Q$ and is well approximated at $Q \\gg 1$ by the formula\n\n$$\n\\sigma (\\tau) \\approx \\pi \\sigma_ {0} \\ln (1 + 2 Q | \\cos \\tau |).\n$$\n\nThe total cross section averaged over time may also be of interest,\n\n$$\n\\overline {{\\sigma}} (Q) = \\int_ {0} ^ {2 \\pi} \\sigma (\\tau) \\frac {d \\tau}{2 \\pi} = \\pi \\sigma_ {0} \\int_ {0} ^ {1} [ 1 - J _ {0} (Q y) ] \\frac {d y}{y}. \\tag {21}\n$$\n\nThe dependence of $\\overline{\\Sigma}_{tot}(Q) = \\overline{\\sigma}(Q) / \\sigma_0$ on $Q$ is shown in\n\nFig. 3. The time-averaged cross section grows logarith-  \n![](images/edca25ca30932f8e03b27a90585e5b936b1255ad1c8b8995ae1eeba2bf1f08bc.jpg)\n\n<details>\n<summary>line</summary>",

\sigma_{a}(\vartheta,\tau)/d\vartheta$ on $\vartheta$ for several values of f.

It follows from the asymptotics obtained that for alternating current the total scattering cross section $\sigma(\tau)$ is finite, in contrast to the case of direct current. The main contribution to $\sigma(\tau)$ is given by the region of scattering angles $\theta \sim \theta_{0} (\vartheta \sim 1)$ . We have from (12) for $v/c \ll 1$ ,

$$
\sigma (\tau) = \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {+ \infty} d y [ 1 - \cos \Xi_ {1} (y, \tau) ]
$$

$$
= \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {Q | \cos \tau |} (1 - \cos y) \frac {d y}{y}. \tag {20}
$$

Naturally, there is no asymmetry in $\sigma(\tau)$ . The dependence of $\Sigma_{tot}(\tau)=\sigma(\tau)/\sigma_{0}$ on $\tau$ is shown in Fig.2 for several values of Q.

!

Figure 3. Dependence of $\overline{\Sigma}_{tot} = \overline{\sigma}(Q) / \sigma_0$ on $Q$ .

mically with increasing $Q$ for large $Q$ .

# III. CONCLUSION

The non-stationary Aharonov-Bohm effect is investigated in the non-relativistic approximation. Using the eikonal approach, the differential and total scattering cross sections are found. In contrast to the stationary Aharonov-Bohm effect, the total cross section in the non-stationary case is finite. The main contribution to the scattering cross section comes from the angles $\theta \sim \theta_{0} = \hbar\omega/E \ll 1$ . The differential scattering cross section contains an asymmetry with respect to the replacement $q \rightarrow -q$ . This asymmetry has a maximum at $\theta \sim \theta_{0}$ and decreases rapidly at $\theta \gg \theta_{0}$ and $\theta \ll \theta_{0}$ . The asymmetry in the cross section can be observed as the non-stationary Hall effect, and the total scattering cross section manifests itself in oscillations of the total electron flux.

# ACKNOWLEDGEMENT

The work of Ivan Terekhov was financially supported by the ITMO Fellowship Program.

[1] Y. Aharonov and D. Bohm, Significance of electromagnetic potentials in the Quantum theory, Phys. Rev. 115, 485 (1959).   
[2] M. Peshkin and A. Tonomura, The Aharonov-Bohm Effect, Lecture Notes in Physics 340 (Springer-Verlag, Berlin, 1989).   
[3] B. Lee, E. Yin, T. K. Gustafson, R. Chiao, Analysis of Aharonov-Bohm effect due to time-dependent vector potentials, Phys. Rev. A 45, 4319 (1992).   
[4] A. N. Ageev, S. Yu. Davydov, and A. G. Chirkov, Magnetic Aharonov-Bohm effect under time-dependent vector potential, Pis'ma v Zhurnal Tekhnicheskoi Fiziki, 9, 70 (2000) [Technical Physics Letters 26, 392 (2000)].   
[5] B. Gaveau, A. M. Nounou, L. S.

Figure 2. Dependence of $\Sigma_{tot}(\tau)=\sigma(\tau)/\sigma_{0}$ on $\tau$ for Q=1 (solid curve), Q=2 (dashed curve) and Q=3 (dotted curve).

The total cross section increases with $Q$ and is well approximated at $Q \gg 1$ by the formula

$$
\sigma (\tau) \approx \pi \sigma_ {0} \ln (1 + 2 Q | \cos \tau |).
$$

The total cross section averaged over time may also be of interest,

$$
\overline {{\sigma}} (Q) = \int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi} \sigma (\tau) \frac {d \tau}{2 \pi} = \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {1} [ 1 - J _ {0} (Q y) ] \frac {d y}{y}. \tag {21}
$$

It follows from the asymptotics obtained that for alternating current the total scattering cross section $\sigma(\tau)$ is finite, in contrast to the case of direct current. The main contribution to $\sigma(\tau)$ is given by the region of scattering angles $\theta \sim \theta_{0} (\vartheta \sim 1)$ . We have from (12) for $v/c \ll 1$ ,

$$
\sigma (\tau) = \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {+ \infty} d y [ 1 - \cos \Xi_ {1} (y, \tau) ]
$$

$$
= \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {Q | \cos \tau |} (1 - \cos y) \frac {d y}{y}. \tag {20}
$$

Naturally, there is no asymmetry in $\sigma(\tau)$ . The dependence of $\Sigma_{tot}(\tau)=\sigma(\tau)/\sigma_{0}$ on $\tau$ is shown in Fig.2 for several values of Q.

, while $G_{2}(\vartheta, \tau)$ does not change sign. For convenience, in Eq. (16) we have passed from the angle $\theta$ to $\vartheta$ .

If $\vartheta \gg 1$ ( $1 \gg \theta \gg \theta_0$ ), then

$$
d \sigma (\vartheta , \tau) = \sigma_ {0} \sin^ {2} (Q \cos \tau) \frac {d \vartheta}{\vartheta^ {2}}. \tag {17}
$$

For $\vartheta \ll 1$ ( $\theta \ll \theta_0$ ), we have

$$
d \sigma (\vartheta , \tau) = \sigma_ {0} \left| \int_ {0} ^ {Q | \cos \tau |} (1 - \cos y) \frac {d y}{y} \right| ^ {2} d \vartheta .

Figure 3. Dependence of $\overline{\Sigma}_{tot} = \overline{\sigma}(Q) / \sigma_0$ on $Q$ .

mically with increasing $Q$ for large $Q$ .

# III. CONCLUSION

The non-stationary Aharonov-Bohm effect is investigated in the non-relativistic approximation. Using the eikonal approach, the differential and total scattering cross sections are found. In contrast to the stationary Aharonov-Bohm effect, the total cross section in the non-stationary case is finite. The main contribution to the scattering cross section comes from the angles $\theta \sim \theta_{0} = \hbar\omega/E \ll 1$ . The differential scattering cross section contains an asymmetry with respect to the replacement $q \rightarrow -q$ . This asymmetry has a maximum at $\theta \sim \theta_{0}$ and decreases rapidly at $\theta \gg \theta_{0}$ and $\theta \ll \theta_{0}$ . The asymmetry in the cross section can be observed as the non-stationary Hall effect, and the total scattering cross section manifests itself in oscillations of the total electron flux.

# ACKNOWLEDGEMENT

The work of Ivan Terekhov was financially supported by the ITMO Fellowship Program.

[1] Y. Aharonov and D. Bohm, Significance of electromagnetic potentials in the Quantum theory, Phys. Rev. 115, 485 (1959).   
[2] M. Peshkin and A. Tonomura, The Aharonov-Bohm Effect, Lecture Notes in Physics 340 (Springer-Verlag, Berlin, 1989).   
[3] B. Lee, E. Yin, T. K. Gustafson, R. Chiao, Analysis of Aharonov-Bohm effect due to time-dependent vector potentials, Phys. Rev. A 45, 4319 (1992).   
[4] A. N. Ageev, S. Yu. Davydov, and A. G. Chirkov, Magnetic Aharonov-Bohm effect under time-dependent vector potential, Pis'ma v Zhurnal Tekhnicheskoi Fiziki, 9, 70 (2000) [Technical Physics Letters 26, 392 (2000)].   
[5] B. Gaveau, A. M. Nounou, L. S.

Figure 2. Dependence of $\Sigma_{tot}(\tau)=\sigma(\tau)/\sigma_{0}$ on $\tau$ for Q=1 (solid curve), Q=2 (dashed curve) and Q=3 (dotted curve).

The total cross section increases with $Q$ and is well approximated at $Q \gg 1$ by the formula

$$
\sigma (\tau) \approx \pi \sigma_ {0} \ln (1 + 2 Q | \cos \tau |).
$$

The total cross section averaged over time may also be of interest,

$$
\overline {{\sigma}} (Q) = \int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi} \sigma (\tau) \frac {d \tau}{2 \pi} = \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {1} [ 1 - J _ {0} (Q y) ] \frac {d y}{y}. \tag {21}
$$

$$
\sigma (\tau) = \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {+ \infty} d y [ 1 - \cos \Xi_ {1} (y, \tau) ]
$$

$$
= \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {Q | \cos \tau |} (1 - \cos y) \frac {d y}{y}. \tag {20}
$$

, while $G_{2}(\vartheta, \tau)$ does not change sign. For convenience, in Eq. (16) we have passed from the angle $\theta$ to $\vartheta$ .

If $\vartheta \gg 1$ ( $1 \gg \theta \gg \theta_0$ ), then

$$
d \sigma (\vartheta , \tau) = \sigma_ {0} \sin^ {2} (Q \cos \tau) \frac {d \vartheta}{\vartheta^ {2}}. \tag {17}
$$

For $\vartheta \ll 1$ ( $\theta \ll \theta_0$ ), we have

$$
d \sigma (\vartheta , \tau) = \sigma_ {0} \left| \int_ {0} ^ {Q | \cos \tau |} (1 - \cos y) \frac {d y}{y} \right| ^ {2} d \vartheta .

Figure 3. Dependence of $\overline{\Sigma}_{tot} = \overline{\sigma}(Q) / \sigma_0$ on $Q$ .

mically with increasing $Q$ for large $Q$ .

# III. CONCLUSION

The non-stationary Aharonov-Bohm effect is investigated in the non-relativistic approximation. Using the eikonal approach, the differential and total scattering cross sections are found. In contrast to the stationary Aharonov-Bohm effect, the total cross section in the non-stationary case is finite. The main contribution to the scattering cross section comes from the angles $\theta \sim \theta_{0} = \hbar\omega/E \ll 1$ . The differential scattering cross section contains an asymmetry with respect to the replacement $q \rightarrow -q$ . This asymmetry has a maximum at $\theta \sim \theta_{0}$ and decreases rapidly at $\theta \gg \theta_{0}$ and $\theta \ll \theta_{0}$ . The asymmetry in the cross section can be observed as the non-stationary Hall effect, and the total scattering cross section manifests itself in oscillations of the total electron flux.

# ACKNOWLEDGEMENT

The work of Ivan Terekhov was financially supported by the ITMO Fellowship Program.

[1] Y. Aharonov and D. Bohm, Significance of electromagnetic potentials in the Quantum theory, Phys. Rev. 115, 485 (1959).   
[2] M. Peshkin and A. Tonomura, The Aharonov-Bohm Effect, Lecture Notes in Physics 340 (Springer-Verlag, Berlin, 1989).   
[3] B. Lee, E. Yin, T. K. Gustafson, R. Chiao, Analysis of Aharonov-Bohm effect due to time-dependent vector potentials, Phys. Rev. A 45, 4319 (1992).   
[4] A. N. Ageev, S. Yu. Davydov, and A. G. Chirkov, Magnetic Aharonov-Bohm effect under time-dependent vector potential, Pis'ma v Zhurnal Tekhnicheskoi Fiziki, 9, 70 (2000) [Technical Physics Letters 26, 392 (2000)].   
[5] B. Gaveau, A. M. Nounou, L. S.

The asymmetry in the cross section can be observed as the non-stationary Hall effect, and the total scattering cross section manifests itself in oscillations of the total electron flux.\n\n# ACKNOWLEDGEMENT\n\nThe work of Ivan Terekhov was financially supported by the ITMO Fellowship Program.\n\n[1] Y.
